opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly I think about it a lot.

The first version of Taichi proved one thing: you can write high-performance parallel code, for physics simulation, graphics, sparse data structures, in a language that feels as easy as Python, and get performance close to hand-tuned CUDA. Many researchers and students started using it, and I'm very grateful for that. But to become a real force in computer science, I think Taichi 2.0 has to go beyond being a nice tool for simulation people.

To me, there are a few key pieces.

First, it should become the default way people think about writing parallel programs. Today, if you want performance, you still have to think about the hardware: threads, memory hierarchy, synchronization, different backends. That's a huge barrier. I'd love a world where a high school student or a domain scientist can just describe the computation, and the compiler takes care of mapping it efficiently to GPUs, CPUs, mobile chips, whatever comes next. Decoupling the algorithm from the data structures and the hardware was the core idea from the beginning, and 2.0 should push that much further.

Second, it has to be truly production-ready, not just a research prototype. That means stability, good tooling, debugging, profiling, and deployment. People should be able to take something written in Taichi and ship it in a game, a mobile app, a VR experience, or an industrial pipeline. Being cool in papers isn't enough; it has to work for millions of users.

Third, it needs to connect with the bigger ecosystem, especially AI. Differentiable programming is something we invested in early, and I think the intersection of physical simulation and machine learning is going to be enormous: digital humans, robotics, generating 3D content. If Taichi becomes the bridge where physics, graphics, and learning come together naturally, that's where it can really matter.

And finally, the community. A language isn't really a language until a lot of people build things you never imagined. If Taichi 2.0 is something where most of the exciting projects come from people I've never met, then I'd consider it a success.

So, in one sentence: Taichi 2.0 should make high-performance visual and physical computing as accessible as writing a Python script, for everyone, on every device. That's the dream.

r001.rationale: The response discusses combining physical simulation with machine learning, but does not propose a hybrid simulator with data-driven neural-network components.

r002.rationale: It describes Taichi as a potential bridge for bringing physical simulation and learning together.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually. Let me take a step back first.

Taichi today is, at its core, a domain-specific language embedded in Python for high-performance parallel computing, especially for things like physical simulation, graphics, and more recently differentiable programming. People write Python-looking code, we JIT-compile it to CPUs and GPUs, and they get performance that's close to hand-written CUDA without having to be a CUDA expert. That's been the value proposition for 1.x.

For a "2.0" that really becomes a major force, I think there are three things that have to happen.

The first is that Taichi needs to stop being a tool only for people who already know they want to write a simulation. Right now, our users are mostly graphics researchers, people doing MPM or SPH or fluid solvers, robotics folks. That's a wonderful community but it's small. The bigger opportunity is that there's an enormous amount of computation in the world that is irregular, sparse, or stateful, and that simply doesn't map well onto the dense tensor abstractions that PyTorch or JAX give you. Think of things like spatially sparse data structures, particle systems, mesh processing, collision detection, even certain kinds of graph algorithms. A Taichi 2.0 should be the default answer when somebody says "my problem doesn't fit in a matrix multiply." If we can be the layer that sits beside the deep learning frameworks and handles everything they're bad at, that's a genuinely large role in the ecosystem.

The second thing is about the compiler. The original Taichi compiler was honestly written by a grad student under deadline pressure, which is me, and it shows in places. A 2.0 needs a much more principled intermediate representation, probably something closer to MLIR-style dialects, so that we can do real optimizations across kernels, fuse operations, and reason about memory layout and data structure choices automatically. One of the original ideas in my thesis was decoupling data structures from computation, so you could swap from a dense array to a hierarchical sparse grid without rewriting your algorithm. That idea is still underexploited. If the compiler could actually search over those layouts and pick the best one for your hardware, that's the kind of leap that makes people in the systems community pay attention.

And then the third piece, which is maybe the hardest, is portability and deployment. Writing the kernel is only half the story. People want to run that same code on an NVIDIA GPU in the lab, on an Apple M-series chip on their laptop, on a phone, in a web browser through WebGPU, inside a game engine. We've done some of this with the ahead-of-time compilation work, but it's still clunky. A real 2.0 would make "write once, run everywhere at high performance" actually true, not just a slogan. If a researcher can prototype a differentiable simulator in a Jupyter notebook and then ship exactly that kernel inside a robotics controller or a mobile app, that closes a loop that nobody closes well today.

If I'm being a bit more ambitious, I'd add a fourth: differentiable programming as a first-class citizen, not a feature bolted on top. Our autodiff was one of the things that got people excited early, with DiffTaichi, but it has lots of restrictions. A 2.0 where you can differentiate through arbitrary control flow, sparse data structures, and even collision and contact in a robust way would be a big deal for robotics, for inverse design, for learning physics from data.

So to summarize, I'd say Taichi 2.0 becomes a major force if it's the thing you reach for whenever your computation is irregular, if the compiler is smart enough to make the hard performance decisions for you, and if the result runs anywhere. Any one of those alone is incremental. All three together, I think, change how a lot of people write software.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulation, differentiable programming, and learning physics from data, but does not propose a hybrid simulator combining simulation with neural-network components.

r002.rationale: It describes Taichi as a layer beside deep-learning frameworks for irregular computation, but does not identify it as infrastructure integrating simulation and neural networks.

astra-6.text:
I think Taichi 2.0 would make high-performance computing accessible to a much broader group of people. You should be able to describe the computation you want in a simple way, and let the system figure out how to execute it efficiently on different hardware.

But I wouldn’t measure success only by how fast a particular benchmark runs. I’d ask: can someone build something with Taichi that they otherwise couldn’t build? Can a researcher try a new idea without spending months optimizing low-level code? Can a small team create a sophisticated simulation without needing a whole team of GPU experts?

If we can make that experience work across a broad range of problems, then Taichi becomes more than a tool for writing fast kernels. It becomes a foundation that other people build on. To me, that would be the meaningful step toward Taichi 2.0.

r001.rationale: The response discusses accessible high-performance computing and simulation, but does not propose a hybrid simulator combining simulation with neural-network components.

r002.rationale: It describes Taichi as a possible foundation others could build on, but does not identify it as infrastructure for integrating simulation and neural networks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Taichi 2.0 should make high-performance computing accessible to a much broader group of people. You should be able to describe the computation you want in a simple way, and the compiler should take care of mapping it efficiently to the hardware. You shouldn’t need to be an expert in every GPU architecture to get good performance.

To become a major force in computer science, though, it needs to go beyond making individual programs faster. It needs to become something people can build on—a foundation for new simulation tools, graphics applications, and other kinds of computational software. For me, the exciting milestone would be people creating things with Taichi that we, as its developers, never anticipated.

r001.rationale: The response discusses accessible high-performance computing and Taichi as a foundation for simulation and graphics software, but does not propose combining simulation with data-driven neural-network components.

r002.rationale: It presents Taichi as infrastructure for computational software generally, without identifying integration between simulation and neural networks.
